impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method-of-treatment claims requires the specification to enable the full scope of the functionally defined genus of antibodies recited in the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding sustains overly broad claims, undermines medical innovation, and conflicts with Supreme Court enablement precedent. The denial preserves a potentially permissive enablement standard for method-of-treatment claims with broad functional genus limitations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting broad method-of-treatment claims covering functional classes of biologics benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, potentially strengthening patent portfolios covering antibody-based therapies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader patent exclusivity periods for biologic drugs, potentially increasing barriers to market entry and litigation risk when challenging enablement of broad method claims.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework for determining a reference patent's prior art date under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2)—which requires only that the provisional application describe the subject matter relied upon rather than support a claim via written description—is correct, or whether Dynamic Drinkware's stricter written-description analysis applies under the AIA.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding of obviousness and remanded for further consideration, addressing the critical question of how to determine a reference patent's effective filing date for prior art purposes under the AIA. The case challenges the Board's Penumbra precedent, which applies a more lenient standard than Dynamic Drinkware for backdating a reference to its provisional application's filing date. The outcome will significantly affect what qualifies as prior art in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit if the Federal Circuit ultimately requires stricter written-description support for backdating references, reducing the prior art available to IPR petitioners challenging patent validity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR challenges face uncertainty about the prior art landscape if the standard for backdating reference patents to provisional filing dates is tightened.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on dissimilarities between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on the design patent infringement test, with Chief Judge Moore and three other judges dissenting or noting dissent. The denial preserves the current Egyptian Goddess framework, which allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment by finding designs sufficiently distinct without detailed prior art analysis. The sharp division signals ongoing doctrinal tension in design patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the current framework's allowance of summary judgment resolution when designs are sufficiently different, reducing litigation costs in design patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that may overemphasize differences between designs, making it harder to prove infringement and potentially devaluing design patent portfolios.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to constitute a virtual assignment, entitling the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the license automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling it to sue without joining A&M. The court also held the license did not automatically terminate when TexasLDPC shifted to enforcement activities. This decision clarifies the standing rights of exclusive licensees and the viability of university patent licensing arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clearer standards confirming their standing to enforce patents independently, and university technology transfer offices gain confidence that their licensing structures will be upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose an avenue for challenging standing of exclusive licensees as a defense to patent infringement suits, particularly where the licensee's primary business is enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the trade secret plaintiff's damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract and reinstated the jury's damages award, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. The decision provides important guidance on acceptable damages methodologies in complex software trade secret cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the appellate court's willingness to revisit excluded damages models and from the reinstatement of the jury's contract damages award, potentially expanding recoverable damages in software misappropriation cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal software after licensing third-party technology face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potential exposure to broader damages theories on remand.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages award was supported by sufficient evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a split decision on patent eligibility of communication technology patents, vacating eligibility for some claims while affirming it for others. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL of non-infringement and the damages verdict. The decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo eligibility framework as applied to telecommunications standards-related patents, distinguishing between claims that recite abstract mathematical concepts and those tied to specific technological implementations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners in the telecommunications and standards-essential patent space gain clearer guidance on structuring claims to survive eligibility challenges, particularly when claims are tied to specific implementations rather than abstract concepts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards face continued patent exposure for standards-related patents that survive eligibility review, and the partial vacatur creates uncertainty about the scope of eligible claims.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient detail in denying a motion for attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions when the patent holder had notice of § 101 eligibility problems from PTO rejections of related applications before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of fees and sanctions, requiring more detailed analysis. The case involved a patent holder that filed suit despite the PTO's repeated § 101 rejections of claims in related applications and a prior district court invalidation of a parent patent. The decision reinforces that courts must adequately explain their reasoning when declining to award fees in cases with strong indicia of exceptional circumstances.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain stronger tools to recover attorney fees when patent holders pursue infringement claims despite substantial evidence of patent ineligibility, deterring weak patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater risk of fee-shifting when asserting patents related to applications or patents that have been rejected or invalidated on § 101 grounds, even if the specific patent asserted has not been so challenged.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and imposed sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 against both the plaintiff and its counsel in a patent infringement case dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without leave to amend, its award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel under § 1927 and the court's inherent power. The court found the plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint and that the proposed amended complaint was futile. The decision reinforces accountability for patent plaintiffs and their attorneys who bring meritless infringement claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strengthened fee-shifting and sanctions precedent that deters frivolous patent suits and holds counsel personally accountable for pursuing baseless claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial risk when filing infringement actions that are subject to dismissal, particularly where pre-suit damages require specific pleading of notice.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute between T-Mobile and KAIFI concerning the meaning of 'survives the EPR' in their patent settlement agreement, transferring the case to the Fifth Circuit. The court reasoned that the dispute was fundamentally about contract interpretation under state law and did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question, despite both parties arguing Federal Circuit jurisdiction existed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties drafting patent settlement agreements gain clarity that disputes over contingent payment terms may be resolved in regional circuits under state contract law, potentially offering more predictable outcomes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies involved in patent settlements face jurisdictional uncertainty when disputes arise over agreement terms linked to PTO proceedings, potentially increasing litigation costs from jurisdictional challenges and transfers.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed 'internal diameter' in oil and gas tool patent claims and whether sufficient evidence supported the jury's infringement and validity findings.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment finding infringement and validity of claims in a patent directed to float tools used in oil well casing operations, and remanded for further proceedings. The case involves significant claim construction disputes relevant to the oil and gas industry's downhole tool patents. The decision highlights the importance of precise claim construction for mechanical patents in the energy sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas equipment space benefit from the Federal Circuit's rigorous review of claim construction, potentially narrowing the scope of competitor patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy technology sector face risk that broadly construed claims may be narrowed on appeal, potentially undermining infringement verdicts and licensing positions.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in a sunset review within 15 days of the notice of initiation conflicts with the governing statute, which imposes no express deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in antidumping sunset reviews is a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. The statute is silent on the specific deadline, and Commerce's regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking. This restores Commerce's ability to enforce participation deadlines that affect whether antidumping duties are revoked.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from the restoration of Commerce's regulatory framework for sunset reviews, which helps ensure continued antidumping protection against foreign competitors when domestic parties timely participate.
impacts.negativeImplications: Importers and foreign producers face continued antidumping duties where domestic parties meet the 15-day deadline, and may lose arguments that the regulatory deadline is ultra vires.
